content:
By the way, I run a semi-secret annual festival for Canadian rationalists. I try to keep the cost of attendance down, and I don't advertise it much outside of the group chats of the established meetup groups in the area (Waterloo, Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal). To even know where the ticket page is, you will need to be reasonably plugged into the IRL Canadian rat scene.1

To me, each year's festival feels a little like a cozy extended family reunion: every so often, a regular of one city will move to another, and it's a good opportunity for them to catch up with old friends and introduce them to new ones. We also have at least a few ex-regulars fly in from the Bay each year.

Well-meaning, economically minded friends tell me to charge more for tickets, and to advertise it more broadly. But I think this will make the festival worse.

Willingness to pay is a useful measure when you don't have higher quality ones available. But, like, I know a bunch of the Canadian rationalists. I was a regular for a bit in Ottawa, ran meetups in Waterloo, and now live in Toronto. And I keep bumping into Montreal rats on the broader festival circuit.

I know which people would be actively excited to come hang out, and which ones will be less enthusiastic about the venture. And some in the former group have basically no money, while some in the latter group have lots to spare. I would much rather gate attendance based on excitement and pre-existing commitment to the scene, and am lucky in that I am information-rich enough to be capable of doing so.

Another recurring festival that happens in my neck of the woods is Dashcon 2 — the recently revived unofficial tumblr convention. The organizers of the tumblr convention, appropriately, are disinclined to believe in market-clearing prices and have done as much as possible to make their ticket pricing accessible (i.e. cheap as hell), despite outsized demand for their product. The end result for both years they've run so far is that they crash the ticketing platform they use and sell out of tickets in ten minutes flat.

In an important way, this has worked out wonderfully in their favour: I've never seen a more enthusiastic, energetic, elaborately-cosplayed set of con attendees. This happens because they are limiting their tickets to only the most eager of their potential attendees — those who are willing to set a phone alarm to open up their ticketing website on a plethora of devices with their payment info ready to go, and panickedly hustle through filling out the payment form in the early hours of the day. But they are also selecting for attendees with the most slack and resources in their lives, and perhaps there are other things the organizers would rather select for.

When there is outsized demand for a thing, consider that it's sort of like having a budget of pretty extensible ways that you can use to whittle down who you want your customers/participants to be. You can set a market-clearing monetary price if you like, but sometimes you are lucky enough to have other options available. Can you select for enthusiasm? Talent? Duration in the community?

If you don't do this selection actively, sometimes it will happen for you anyways.

After moving from a city of almost 700,000 to a city of more than seven million, the attendance of my weekly meetups has increased only modestly. This was surprising to me at first, but now I have a good story for why this might have been the case: I require people to do readings and come to the meetups ready to discuss them, and the opportunity cost of homework is greater in a big city than it is in a college town. The enthusiasm that's required to attend is higher, such that a smaller percentage of potential attendees clear the market.

Eliot, who runs meetups in Australia, likes to describe his philosophy in the following way: "I believe in having wide open doors that are out of the way. That way people are already selected for door finding." I really like this.

Incidentally, a similar dynamic is why I like mostly writing here, on a blog that is out of the spotlight. I want the people who read me to have been pre-selected for.





  1. If you are Canadian and interested in attending, but you don't live in a city with an extant meetup group, message me and I'll see what I can do.↩
